result.summary: Pausanias walks the road from Mycenae toward Argos, noting the hero-chapel of Perseus, the tomb of Thyestes, and a roofless temple of Demeter. He then turns to the Argive royal houses, the three kingdoms, and how the Heraclidae displaced Tisamenus and the Nestor family.

scenes.title: Perseus' shrine and Thyestes' tomb
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the shrine of Perseus and the tomb of Thyestes, and recounts the feud of Atreus and Thyestes. He reflects on inherited family guilt.

scenes.title: Mysian Demeter and the Inachus
scenes.summary: Further along are the temple of Mysian Demeter, the river Inachus, an altar of the Sun and the gate of Ilithyia.

scenes.title: Argive kingdoms and Orestes
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains the division of Argos into three kingdoms after the women's madness, and the descent of the kings to Orestes and Tisamenus.
scenes.stakes: Control of the Argive kingdom passes among rival royal lines.

scenes.title: Return of the Heraclidæ
scenes.summary: The Heraclidae return and claim Argos and Lacedaemon, driving out Tisamenus and the Nestor descendants, who go to Achaia and Athens. Melanthus becomes king at Athens.
scenes.stakes: Tisamenus and the Neleids lose their kingdoms to the returning Heraclidae.

analysis.text: Pausanias links landmarks to inherited guilt and royal succession, showing how Argive history is read off the landscape.
The Heraclidae's claim to Argos reflects the Greek tradition of the Dorian 'Return', used to legitimise Dorian rule in the Peloponnese.

language_notes.text: A hero-chapel is a small shrine where a hero, a mortal honoured after death, received cult offerings.
Dictys and Clymene: the fisherman and his wife who, in the myth, rescued Danae and the infant Perseus from the sea chest at Seriphus.
The golden sheep: a golden lamb from Atreus' flock. Thyestes took it with the help of Atreus' wife Aerope, whose seduction gave him the means.
The 'law of Tit for Tat' means strict retaliation in kind; Atreus is said to have gone far beyond it.
Glaucus asked the Delphic oracle whether he could keep money entrusted to him by swearing falsely. The Pythia warned that his descendants would be punished.
'Host' here means one who entertained the goddess as a guest, a common origin story for cult titles.
The madness of the Argive women is the myth of the Proetides: women driven mad, whom the seer Melampus cured in return for a share of the kingdom.
"Ilium" is Troy; Amphilochus left Argos after the Trojan War to settle in the region later called Amphilochia.
Hercules was said to have helped Tyndareus by defeating Hippocoon, who had driven him from Sparta; the Heraclidæ cite this as a precedent for their claim.
"Pæonidæ" and "Alcmæonidæ" are Athenian families named for Pæon and Alcmæon, descendants of Nestor's line.

context_notes.text: Perseus was honoured at Seriphus, the island where he grew up and later turned King Polydectes to stone with Medusa's head.
Pelops killed the charioteer Myrtilus, who cursed his house. This curse was blamed for the crimes of Atreus and Thyestes.
The Inachus was the chief river of the Argolid, named for a river-god regarded as an early king of Argos.
Argos lay in the northeastern Peloponnese. Pausanias uses the three-kingdom division as a mark of its unusual political history.
Cinæthon was an early Greek epic poet of Lacedaemon, cited by Pausanias for genealogies.
Pelops's line (Atreus, Agamemnon, Orestes) ruled Argos; the Heraclidæ descended from Perseus, an earlier Argive king, hence their claim.
Melanthus came from Nestor's Pylian family and became king of Athens, replacing Thymœtes, last of Theseus's line.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a cautious, humane investigator, refusing to condemn the family and showing his reflective, personal stance.
He compares the family's suffering to the oracle given to Glaucus, using it to suggest guilt passing down through generations.
Pausanias gives the myth briefly and matter-of-factly as history, treating legendary cures and kingships as established fact.
The phrase "it seems to me" shows Pausanias the traveller-historian giving his own judgment on the claim.
The long chain of fathers and sons shows Pausanias's genealogical method, defining each person by his descent.
